common_name: Barton Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming Pure White Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in fall or early spring in partial shade with moist, acidic, well-drained soil; Barton is an old southern selection prized for its large, overlapping, pure white bracts.

directions: Barton produces an unusually heavy display of large, overlapping white bracts each spring, ranking among the showiest of the older named white-flowering dogwood selections for southern gardens. Site it in dappled or partial shade with rich, acidic, evenly moist soil, since full-sun exposure in hot climates stresses the shallow root system and increases susceptibility to leaf scorch and powdery mildew. Maintain a wide mulch ring to buffer soil temperature swings and conserve moisture, and avoid soil compaction or turf competition near the trunk. Fall brings reddish-purple foliage and clusters of red drupes that draw songbirds through winter.

common_name: Weaver's White Dogwood (Large-Bracted Southern-Adapted White Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Weaver's White is noted for strong performance and reliable flowering in zones 8-9 where straight-species dogwood can struggle with heat.

directions: Weaver's White is valued for its unusually good heat adaptation, flowering reliably across the warmer end of the species' range where many white dogwood selections falter under summer stress. Its large, overlapping bracts open in mid-spring ahead of most foliage, and the tree can be trained to a single leader or allowed to develop the informal, multi-trunked form the species takes on naturally. Provide consistent moisture during establishment and mulch generously, since dogwood roots run shallow and dry out quickly in compacted or exposed soil. Red-to-maroon fall color and persistent red fruit extend the ornamental season into winter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with some protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the variegated leaf margins; Rainbow is a slower-growing, smaller-statured selection suited to specimen placement in modest-sized gardens.

directions: Rainbow carries green leaves edged in bright yellow through spring and summer, shifting to red and purple tones in fall for a long season of foliage color that is arguably more dramatic than its floriferous white bracts and glossy crimson fruit. Choose a site with morning sun and afternoon shade or high dappled light, since intense direct sun can scorch the thinner variegated leaf tissue while deep shade dulls the color contrast. It grows more slowly and stays more compact than straight-species dogwood, making it a good fit for foundation plantings or small woodland-edge gardens where a full-sized shade tree would overwhelm the space. Keep soil consistently moist and mulched, and avoid root disturbance once established.

common_name: Welchii Tricolor Dogwood (Green-Cream-Pink Variegated Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with shelter from harsh midday sun and wind, both of which can burn the delicate tricolor leaf margins; Welchii is grown primarily for foliage rather than flower display.

directions: Welchii is grown chiefly for its striking tricolor foliage, with leaves splashed in green, creamy white, and pink that shift toward reddish-purple as the season progresses, making it one of the most distinctive foliage dogwoods available. White spring bracts appear against the emerging variegated leaves, but the ongoing foliage display is the main draw through summer and into fall. Site it out of drying wind and the most intense afternoon sun to prevent leaf-margin scorch, and keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist in acidic, well-drained soil. This selection is noted for good tolerance of verticillium wilt, a soil-borne disease that can afflict dogwood planted in former vegetable garden sites.

common_name: Sweetwater Red Dogwood (Deep Red-Bracted Burgundy-Fall-Foliage Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with moist, acidic soil; Sweetwater Red is an upright, rounded selection prized for deep red bracts and burgundy fall foliage.

directions: Sweetwater Red produces vivid red bracts in early to mid spring on an upright, tidily rounded framework, then follows with foliage that deepens to rich burgundy well before most other dogwood cultivars begin to color. Grow it in partial shade with organically rich, consistently moist, acidic soil, and mulch broadly to protect the shallow root system from summer heat and drought. It tends to hold a neater, more uniform habit than seedling-grown red dogwoods, making it a good choice where a compact, well-shaped specimen is wanted near a patio or entry planting. Glossy red fruit ripens in fall and is quickly taken by songbirds.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Environmental Horticulture

common_name: Purple Glory Dogwood (Red-Bracted Purple-Black Foliage Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with rich, acidic, well-drained soil; Purple Glory was selected as a chance seedling in Tennessee for its unusual season-long purple foliage progression.

directions: Purple Glory offers a foliage progression unlike most flowering dogwood cultivars: light purple new growth in spring deepens to dark purple through summer and finishes nearly black-purple in fall, framing long-lasting, showy red bracts that open earlier in the season. Grow it in average to organically rich, medium-moisture, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to part shade, giving it afternoon shade in hotter climates to preserve foliage color and reduce heat stress. A two- to four-inch mulch ring keeps the shallow roots cool and moist and reduces competition from turf or nearby plantings. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood shortly after flowering to preserve next year's buds.

common_name: Appalachian Joy Dogwood (Powdery-Mildew-Resistant Double-Bracted Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in partial shade with rich, moist, acidic soil; Appalachian Joy was released by the University of Tennessee dogwood breeding program for powdery mildew resistance and an unusual supernumerary-bract bloom.

directions: Appalachian Joy was selected from among roughly a million seedlings by University of Tennessee researchers for resistance to powdery mildew, one of the most persistent foliar problems affecting flowering dogwood in humid regions, while also displaying an unusual supernumerary bloom in which many flowers carry extra, doubled bracts for a fuller spring display. Plant in partial shade with rich, evenly moist, acidic soil, and mulch well to buffer the shallow root zone against heat and drought. Fall brings a strong transition through scarlet, burgundy, and deep red foliage tones alongside clusters of bright red fruit that persist into winter and feed songbirds. Choose this selection over unimproved seedling dogwood where powdery mildew has been a recurring problem in the landscape.
sources: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture

common_name: Karen's Appalachian Blush Dogwood (Pink-Edged White-Bracted Mildew-Resistant Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in sun to dappled shade with rich, acidic, moist soil; Karen's Appalachian Blush is a University of Tennessee introduction chosen as a chance seedling for its pink-edged bracts and superior powdery mildew resistance among white dogwoods.

directions: Karen's Appalachian Blush opens large, loosely overlapping white bracts finely edged in pink each spring, a soft two-tone effect distinct from the solid white or solid pink bracts of most flowering dogwood cultivars. It was selected in Tennessee in part for powdery mildew resistance reported to exceed that of other white-flowering dogwood, an important advantage in humid climates where mildew disfigures foliage late in the season. Grow in sun to dappled shade in rich, well-drained, consistently moist, acidic soil, and mulch to protect the shallow roots through heat and dry spells. Glossy red fruit persists into winter and draws overwintering songbirds, and reddish-purple fall foliage rounds out a long season of interest.

common_name: Autumn Gold Dogwood (Golden Fall Foliage with Gold-Orange Winter Twigs)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in sun to dappled shade with rich, moist, well-drained acidic soil; Autumn Gold is a Don Shadow selection valued for reliable golden fall color and colorful winter twigs in addition to disease resistance.

directions: Autumn Gold extends the ornamental season of flowering dogwood well past bloom time, turning a clear buttery gold in fall with pink and orange highlights before finishing in scarlet, and carrying that gold-to-orange color into the winter twigs long after the leaves have dropped. Broad white-bracted flowers appear in May against a backdrop of the same disease resistance breeding that has improved many recent dogwood introductions. Plant in sun to dappled shade in rich, evenly moist, well-drained, acidic soil, and water regularly through the first two seasons while the root system establishes. Red fruit ripening alongside the gold foliage draws bees during bloom and birds once fruit sets, making this a strong multi-season specimen for a lawn edge or mixed border.
